purpose: This medicine is used to treat serious fungal infections, specifically a type called invasive aspergillosis and invasive mucormycosis. These are dangerous infections that usually affect people with weakened immune systems. Your doctor prescribed this because these types of fungal infections need a strong antifungal medicine to get better.
how_it_works: Fungi need a special substance called ergosterol to build their outer walls and survive. This medicine blocks the enzyme that fungi use to make ergosterol. Without it, the fungal cell wall breaks down and the fungus dies, helping your body clear the infection.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, low potassium or magnesium levels in your blood, headache, tiredness, shortness of breath, swelling in the legs or feet, and abnormal liver blood tests. Some people also feel confused or have back pain.
warnings: Tell your doctor right away if you notice yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain, as this could mean liver problems. Do not take this medicine if you are also taking certain other medications like ketoconazole or high doses of ritonavir, as dangerous interactions can occur. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, talk to your doctor because this medicine may harm an unborn baby. This medicine can also affect your heart rhythm, so let your doctor know if you have a heart condition called short QT syndrome.
typical_dosing: Usually, you start with a loading dose — two capsules (372 mg each) taken three times a day, about 8 hours apart, for the first two days (6 doses total). After that, you take one capsule (372 mg) once a day. The capsules are swallowed whole and can be taken with or without food. If you take the IV (intravenous) version in the hospital, your care team will handle the dosing for you.
